findings.body:
Null IDP removal can throw before delegate returns false

`storedIdp` is read directly from the delegate and may be null when `remove` is called for a non-existent alias. The new unconditional `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` then calls the login predicate with null; because the new predicate subsequently dereferences `idp.getOrganizationId()`, this can throw a NullPointerException instead of preserving the existing `false` return behavior from `idpDelegate.remove(alias)`. This also applies if the alias cache had no entry. Guard the login invalidation (or make the predicate null-safe across all clauses) before delegating removal.

Cached org-disabled IDPs are not invalidated on org state changes

This skip assumes a login-qualified IDP with the same organization id does not affect the cached login results. However `getForLogin` returns organization-aware models whose `isEnabled()` depends on the organization and provider state, and the service layer now re-filters `idp.isEnabled()` after fetching from this cache. If an organization linked to a public IDP is disabled/re-enabled, `registerOrganizationInvalidation` only invalidates the org and `getByOrganization` key, not the `.idp.login.*` keys. Existing login caches can therefore continue to serve IDs for providers whose wrapper now evaluates disabled (or omit them after re-enable) until an IDP change happens. The login caches need to be invalidated when organization state affecting provider availability changes, or the cache lookup needs to account for org invalidation.

Cleanup registers the literal alias instead of the created IDP

The new test creates providers named `idp-alias-0` ... `idp-alias-19`, but each cleanup uses `testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove`. That resource does not correspond to any of the providers just created, so the test leaks all of these IDPs into the realm and can make later tests order-dependent. The same mistake appears for `idp-alias-20` below. Capture the actual alias used for each provider and register cleanup for that alias.

getBouncyCastleProvider can recursively initialize BouncyIntegration

This method calls `KeyStore.getDefaultType()`, which resolves `KeyStore.getDefaultType`'s implementation through security properties and can trigger `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` initialization in code paths that already use `CryptoIntegration.init`. Since `BouncyIntegration.loadProvider()` calls `CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider()`, returning a provider by constructing a KeyStore is risky here and can fail during authz client bootstrap. The authz client provider should avoid this BouncyCastle hook entirely (for example by returning null as the Elytron provider does) rather than invoking another crypto API while the global provider is still being initialized.

The existing FIPS provider calls `format.toString()`, and `KeystoreUtil.getKeystoreType` also uses the enum's string value. Using `name()` here makes authz-client private_key_jwt loading inconsistent with the rest of the code and can reject configured PKCS12/P12 stores on providers that expect the canonical type string.

Unlike the built-in `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider`, recovery codes are supposed to be single-use and consumed in order (`getNextRecoveryAuthnCode`/`removeRecoveryAuthnCode`). findings.body:
Denial cache key omits the identity type

The negative cache is keyed only by namespace, UID, action, name, and folder. Different identity types can share the same UID string (for example `anonymous:0` and `render:0`), but they have different authorization semantics. A deny cached for anonymous access to a dashboard will be returned before evaluating renderer permissions and can incorrectly deny `render:0`, which normally has a wildcard read grant. Include the identity type in the denial cache key or keep separate negative caches per identity type.

Cached denials can outlive newly granted permissions

Once a request is denied, future checks for the same resource return false from `permDenialCache` before consulting either the permission cache or the store. This bypasses the new DB fallback path that handles stale positive permission caches, so granting the user access shortly after a deny will still be rejected until this cache entry expires. The negative cache needs explicit invalidation on permission changes, or it should be avoided/validated against the store before denying.

Denial cache key can collide between resources

The key concatenates variable fields with `_`, but dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores. Distinct requests such as name=`dash_a`, parent=`b` and name=`dash`, parent=`a_b` produce the same suffix, so a cached deny for one resource/folder can deny another. Use an unambiguous encoding for each component, such as length-prefixing or escaping, before concatenating.

This is a distinct, plausible correctness/security issue.

findings.body:
Logger interface change breaks existing implementations

Adding FromContext to the public plugins/log.Logger interface is a breaking API change for any existing implementation outside this package (for example wrappers around plugin loggers). Those types will stop compiling even if they do not need contextual logging. Consider avoiding the interface expansion (e.g. use a smaller optional/contextual interface at the call site) or provide an adapter path for existing Logger implementations.

FromContext is not covered by tests for contextual attributes

This wrapper now relies on infra/log.FromContext preserving the plugin logger's identity and adding contextual attributes, but there is no regression coverage for the new behavior. A test should verify both the no-context case and that log.WithContextualAttributes(ctx, ...) is included when logging through pkg/plugins/log.Logger.FromContext; otherwise changes in the wrapper or infra logger could silently drop pluginId/endpoint from backend request logs.

Stream requests do not get contextual logging attributes

The new middleware only instruments QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics. SubscribeStream, PublishStream, and RunStream all have PluginContext too, but are passed through unchanged, so any downstream logs for streaming endpoints will miss pluginId/user/datasource/endpoint attributes while the rest of the client API has them. If this middleware is intended to centralize request context enrichment, the stream methods should be instrumented as well.

LoggerMiddleware context dependency lacks regression coverage

LoggerMiddleware now depends on a prior middleware adding contextual attributes and logs through FromContext, but there are no tests covering this middleware. A regression test should verify that enabled backend request logging still includes status/duration as well as pluginId/endpoint/user/datasource/trace fields when a contextual logger is present; otherwise ordering changes or disabled/missing ContextualLoggerMiddleware can silently remove fields from the audit-style "grafana-data-egress" log.

Middleware instance stores mutable next across requests

NewMetricsMiddleware constructs one *MetricsMiddleware and stores the downstream client in imw.next when CreateClientMiddleware is called. The decorator rebuilds the chain for every request, so concurrent calls mutate and read the same next field on a shared middleware instance, creating a data race and possible cross-request delegation to the wrong client if the middleware is reused. Return a fresh MetricsMiddleware per CreateClientMiddleware call or make next immutable per wrapper instance.

Tests do not cover the new MetricsMiddleware constructor path

The renamed test still bypasses NewMetricsMiddleware by setting mw.next manually on an instance from newMetricsMiddleware. That misses the changed constructor behavior where a single middleware instance with a mutable next field is reused. Add coverage that exercises NewMetricsMiddleware through the decorator (ideally with concurrent requests) so regressions in the public middleware factory are caught.

Contextual logger ordering is easy to regress without tests

The request logger now depends on NewContextualLoggerMiddleware running before it in the client chain to include pluginId/endpoint/user/datasource fields. This stack order is subtle because middlewares are reversed during decoration, and there is no integration test asserting the final backend request log context. A future reorder would silently remove those fields, so please add coverage for CreateMiddlewares ordering/log output.

Failed limit checks poison the device cache

`tagDeviceUI` adds the device ID to the local cache before writing to the store. Now that `TagDevice` returns write errors (including `ErrDeviceLimitReached`), a rejected new device is still cached for 29 minutes. Subsequent requests from the same device skip the store entirely and return nil, allowing anonymous authentication even if the device limit is still exceeded. Remove the cache entry when the write fails so failed tags are retried and continue to enforce the limit.

Proposed patch:
```diff
--- a/pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go
+++ b/pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/impl.go
@@ -144,6 +144,7 @@ func (a *AnonDeviceService) TagDevice(ctx context.Context, httpReq *http.Request
 	err = a.tagDeviceUI(ctx, httpReq, taggedDevice)
 	if err != nil {
 		a.log.Debug("Failed to tag device for UI", "error", err)
+		a.localCache.Delete(taggedDevice.CacheKey())
 		return err
 	}
 

```

Device limit check is not atomic

The limit is enforced by counting active devices and then inserting/upserting in a separate statement. Concurrent first requests can all observe `count < deviceLimit` and then insert, so the number of active anonymous devices can exceed the configured limit. This needs an atomic enforcement strategy (for example a transaction/lock or database-level guard) around the count and insert/update path.

findings.body:
Upsampling decision ignores the split dataset being queried

`should_upsample` is computed from the outer request `dataset`, not the `scoped_dataset` actually passed into `_get_event_stats`. In the dashboard split path, a discover request can call `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., errors_only_query)` for the errors-only branch while the original request query does not contain `event.type:error`. Because `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` still inspects the outer dataset/request instead of the scoped dataset/query being executed, that errors-only query will not be upsampled even when all projects are allowlisted. The same mismatch can make cached split decisions depend on the original request rather than the branch being queried. Consider basing the transform on `scoped_dataset` and the effective `query` argument (or otherwise carrying the split dataset/query context into the helper).

Aliased count axes are not upsampled

The transform only rewrites columns whose normalized string is exactly `count()`. The events stats API supports aliased aggregate axes such as `count() as errors` (the query builder parses `as` aliases), but those columns will be left as raw counts even when the project is allowlisted. This produces inconsistent results depending solely on whether the caller aliases the yAxis, and multi-axis/top-events serialization can commonly rely on stable aliases. The transform should preserve aliases while replacing the aggregate, e.g. rewrite `count() as foo` to `upsampled_count() as foo`.

Internal upsampled_count function is publicly exposed

`upsampled_count` is added to the public Discover function converter without `private=True`, so users can request `upsampled_count()` directly on arbitrary discover queries. That bypasses the allowlist/error-query checks added in the endpoint helper and will query `sample_weight` even for datasets or entities where it may not exist, causing errors or exposing an implementation detail as API surface. Since this function is intended only as an internal rewrite target, it should be marked private and only enabled through the controlled path.

Factory sample-rate derivation accepts invalid values

The new test factory helper sets `sample_rate` for any truthy `client_sample_rate` that can be cast to float, including strings and values outside `(0, 1]`. Production ingestion only accepts numeric values in that range before setting `sample_rate`. This divergence can make tests pass with events/snuba rows that production would never generate (or with nonsensical weights such as negative or >1 sample rates), hiding bugs in the upsampling path. The factory should mirror the production validation instead of swallowing all conversion errors and accepting any truthy float.

Threshold can trip before enough failures exist

When `failure_issue_threshold > 1`, this only checks whether the last up-to-threshold check-ins contain an OK check-in. Backup-code login can bypass password verification

The password check above is skipped whenever `credentials.totpCode` is present. This new backup-code branch only gates on `credentials.backupCode`, so a direct credentials request can include any non-empty `totpCode` plus a valid backup code and authenticate without the account password. Backup codes are a second factor and should still require the primary credential (or reject requests that submit both factors in a way that skips password verification).

Backup code consumption is not atomic

This reads the encrypted code list, checks the code, and then writes back a modified list. Two concurrent login requests with the same backup code can both read the old list before either update commits, both pass `indexOf`, and both authenticate successfully. Since backup codes are intended to be single-use, the consume operation needs to be atomic (for example, a transaction/compare-and-set on the encrypted value or another per-code storage model).

Dismissing backup-code step leaves 2FA state stale

After enabling 2FA the modal now waits on the custom Close button to call `onEnable()`. If the user dismisses the dialog via Esc, outside click, or the dialog close control while backup codes are displayed, `onOpenChange` closes the modal without invalidating the user query or resetting this component state. The database has 2FA enabled, but the switch can remain unchecked and reopening the modal can show the stale backup-code step instead of the current enabled state.
